lesson.title: Encapsulation: Boxing a Message Inside Box After Box
lesson.summary: Encapsulation is the process of wrapping a unit of data with a header, and sometimes a trailer, turning it into the payload of the next layer down.
lesson.body:
Encapsulation is the mechanism that turns the ideas of header and payload into a working system. It is the repeated act of taking whatever data a layer has been given, attaching a header in front of it, sometimes attaching a trailer behind it, and handing the whole result down to the next layer as that layer's payload. Each layer does this without needing to know anything about the meaning of the data it is wrapping. It just adds its own instructions and passes the parcel along.

The reason this matters is that no single piece of hardware or software could realistically handle addressing, reliability, and physical transmission all at once. Encapsulation lets each concern be handled independently, in its own header, at its own layer, while still producing one combined stream of bytes that a physical network can actually transmit. A header, as covered earlier, only means something because a payload sits behind it for it to describe. Encapsulation is what puts that pairing into practice, over and over, at every layer a message passes through.

Walk through a real example step by step. A browser wants to send the message "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" to a web server. First, this text becomes the payload of a TCP segment, and TCP encapsulates it by adding a TCP header containing, among other things, the source and destination port numbers. Next, that entire TCP segment, header and payload together, becomes the payload of an IP packet, and IP encapsulates it by adding an IP header containing the source and destination IP addresses. Finally, that IP packet becomes the payload of an Ethernet frame, and Ethernet encapsulates it by adding both a header, containing physical hardware addresses, and a trailer, containing the frame check sequence described earlier. What began as roughly 25 bytes of text is now wrapped inside three nested layers of headers and one trailer before it ever reaches the cable.

A useful way to picture this is nested envelopes. The HTTP message is a letter. TCP puts that letter in an envelope addressed by port number. IP takes that whole envelope and puts it inside a larger envelope addressed by IP address. Ethernet takes that larger envelope and puts it inside a shipping box addressed by hardware address, sealing the box with a trailer that proves nothing was tampered with in transit. Each layer only ever looks at its own envelope, never opening the ones nested inside it.

This layered wrapping is not extra work invented for its own sake, it is what allows the same underlying physical network to carry web traffic, email, video calls, and file transfers simultaneously, each correctly addressed and handled at every layer, without any layer needing to understand what the others are doing. The natural next question, covered in the following chapter, is what happens to all of this wrapping once the data reaches its destination.
